en: *Gurupañcāśikā*: Om, homage to the Buddha!
Having prostrated according to the ritual rule before the lotus-feet of the Guru, for the sake of attaining the state of the illustrious Vajrasattva;
This stainless service to him, sung in many tantras, is now told in brief; listen with reverence! // 1 //
For the Vajrācārya who has obtained the supreme consecration is worshipped by the Tathāgatas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions, coming at the three times of day. // 2 //
The teacher, the instructor, should be attended upon with supreme devotion three times a day with offerings of flowers and mandalas, and his feet should be saluted with the head.

Whether he be a householder or even a novice, one who places the True Dharma and so forth at the forefront should be saluted by those who uphold the vows with a respectful mind, in order to avoid bringing reproach upon the world.
The observer of the vow should perform everything—such as rising from a comfortable seat, purposeful activity, and showing respect—while omitting ritual worship and prostration. // 5 //
First, the relationship between disciple and teacher must be established by the wise after careful examination;
for it is a fault shared equally by both teacher and disciple if they fall from their commitments.
A wise person should not make someone who is merciless, wrathful, cruel, arrogant, frivolous, unrestrained, and self-exalting either a teacher or a disciple.
Steadfast, disciplined, wise, patient, upright, and free from deceit;
skilled in the application of mantra and tantra, compassionate, and proficient in the treatises. // 8 //
An Ācārya who has full knowledge of the ten principles, is skilled in the work of drawing mandalas, is an expounder of mantras, and is serene with his senses subdued, shall be [the preceptor]. (9)
If a conscious disciple, having become a student, should treat that protector with contempt, he will experience constant suffering due to his insult of all the Buddhas. (10)
That great fool, who reviles the feet of the Guru, dies from calamities, thieves, planetary afflictions, fevers, poisons, and the like. (11)
Slain by royal winds, fires, and serpents, by ḍākinīs, water, and thieves, or even by obstacles and vināyakas, he shall go to hell. (12)
One should never cause agitation in the mind of the preceptor;
when one of poor wisdom does so, he is certainly cooked in hell. (13)
Those hells which are proclaimed as terrifying, beginning with Avīci—residence therein is declared to result from reviling the teacher. (14)
Therefore, with every effort, one should never, under any circumstances, disparage the Vajrācārya, the great guru, who is a sublime and hidden excellence. (15)
By giving sacrificial fees as desired, one becomes devoted and respectful toward the guru;
for once the afflictions such as fever have been addressed, they no longer prevail.

O teacher of self-restraint, one should serve [the guru] even at the cost of one's own children, wife, and other things that are difficult to give away, or even at the cost of one's own life; how much more so, then, with unstable wealth?
For it is because this state of Buddhahood—which is extremely difficult to attain even in tens of millions of incalculable eons—bestows itself upon one who possesses diligence in this very life. (18)
One's own commitment must be maintained constantly; likewise, the Tathāgatas must be worshipped constantly;
and one must constantly give to the guru, for he is equal to all the Buddhas. (19)
Whatever is most dear to one in the world, or whatever is most excellent, that indeed should always be given to the teacher by one who desires imperishability. (20)
What is given to him is as if given eternally to all the Buddhas; and from that accumulation of merit arises supreme enlightenment. 21.
Those disciples, endowed with the qualities of compassion, renunciation, ethical discipline, and patience,
do not conceive of any difference between their guru and Vajradhara.
Out of fear of breaking a shrine or similar offenses, one should not even step over the shadow of the Guru;
what need is there to mention stepping over his sandals, seat, vehicle, or other belongings? (23)
The high-minded one, with a joyful heart, should listen to the teacher’s command with effort;
if he is incapable, he should explain his incapacity to him through logical reasoning.
One attains success through the guru, heaven through the guru, and happiness through the guru;
therefore, with every effort, one should not transgress the command of the guru. // 25 //
One should always remain composed, regarding the Guru’s property as one's own self, the Guru’s wife as one's own mother, and the Guru’s followers as one's own kinsmen.

One should not mount a bed or a superior vehicle, nor wear a turban or similar headgear; nor should one place a foot upon a seat or rest a hand upon the hips while in the presence [of the teacher]. (27)
One should not remain sleeping or sitting when the teacher has risen;
one should always be skillful and full of energy in performing his duties. (28)
One should not discharge phlegm or other secretions, stretch out one's feet, walk about, or engage in dispute in the presence of the guru. (29)
One should not perform massaging, dancing, singing, or playing musical instruments, nor engage in excessive conversation in the presence of the guru. (30)
Having bowed, one should rise from one's seat and sit down with devotion;
at night, in water, or on a dangerous path, one should proceed after requesting [permission] from those in front.
The wise one should not move his limbs, nor should he resort to yawning and the like;
he should not snap his fingers while the Teacher is present before him. (32)
Washing the feet, wiping the limbs, anointing with oil, and massaging should be performed after first prostrating; thereafter, one should do whatever he may command. (33)
During invocations and similar occasions, one should append such terms as "Venerable Feet" (pūjyapāda) to the name of the Guru;
at other times, one may address him with faith using respectful epithets. (34)
"Command me; I shall do it," he should say to the teacher with palms joined;
having heard the command, he should act exactly as instructed without wavering. (35)
When laughter or a cough arises, one should cover the mouth with the hand;
at its conclusion, one should communicate one's intention using gentle words.
Disciplined, one should stand before [the teacher] prepared with the binding of garments and other items;
with knees on the ground and palms joined in *añjali*, one should request three times to listen. (37)
One should always perform virtuous deeds with a mind free from egoism,
restrained by modesty and the fear of sin, like a young bride.
One should not engage in playful or frivolous behavior in the presence of the Teacher;
furthermore, one should thoroughly examine and strictly avoid any other such action. (39)
During the consecration, the mandala ritual, the fire offering, the gathering of disciples, the recitation of narratives, or while residing with the guru, one should always maintain close proximity.
Whatever is obtained during the consecration and other rites, all that one should offer to the guru;
and what is given by him, one should accept for oneself and use to satisfy others as well. (41)
A disciple should never assume the status of being his own teacher;
he should ensure that his own disciple remains distinct from the honors and services due to the guru.
Whatever the teacher may give himself, or whatever the preceptor may cause to be given,
that should be accepted by the wise man with joined palms after having prostrated.
Remaining mindful while diligently performing all his duties, he should dispel [any attachment] toward his own kinsmen with a joyful heart and through love, by means of that very mindfulness.
If one who is authorized by the guru and full of faith does not perform the task,
yet remains ill with a wholesome mind, he does not incur sin in this way.
What else? One should perform whatever is possible for the satisfaction of the guru;
one's conduct should be practiced with diligence and never treated with contempt. 46.
In every way and at all times, accomplishment follows the Ācārya;
the Guru must be propitiated with all things, as stated by Vajradhara. (47)
Having become one of pure intention, the disciple should go for refuge to the Three Jewels;
having studied under the guru, he should recite [the texts] and perform the ritual of renunciation.
Then, having made [the disciple] a vessel for the true Dharma by bestowing the mantras and so forth, one should recite and also cause them to memorize the fourteen root downfalls. (49)

By whatever infinite mass of merit has been accumulated by me through bringing about the increase of all that is wholesome for the faultless disciple who followed his guru—by that may all sentient beings swiftly attain perfect accomplishment, having realized the state of a Sugata. (50)
Thus ends the Fifty Verses on the Guru.
This is the work of the great teacher Aśvaghoṣa.
